questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the correct starting mental model for an endpoint that fronts a language model?
options: It is still an ordinary HTTP API first, requiring the same authentication, rate limiting, input validation, and output handling any API needs, tuned for AI-specific behavior
It needs an entirely new security model with no relationship to standard API security practices
It does not need authentication because the model itself decides who is authorized
It only needs TLS in transit and nothing else, since the model handles all other security internally
questions.explain: An AI endpoint is still an HTTP API — authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and input/output handling all still apply. The lesson covers where AI-specific behavior changes how those fundamentals get tuned, not whether they apply.

questions.q: Why does a traditional fixed requests-per-minute rate limit fail to protect an AI endpoint the way it protects a typical REST API?
options: Because rate limiting is only relevant to databases, not APIs
Because AI endpoints cannot be rate limited by any method

Because a request-count limit assumes similar cost per request, but AI calls vary enormously in compute cost, letting an attacker stay under the limit while running up cost through large-context requests
Because language models never receive more than one request per session
questions.explain: A two-sentence prompt and a context-window-filling prompt both count as 'one request' under a count-based limit, even though their compute cost differs by orders of magnitude — the gap a denial-of-wallet attack exploits.

questions.q: What is a denial-of-wallet attack against an AI endpoint?
options: Using a stolen API key to impersonate an administrator
Stealing a user's payment card number through a vulnerable checkout API
Exhausting a database's storage quota through repeated writes
Sending oversized or expensive requests at a rate that stays under a request-count limit, deliberately running up inference cost rather than taking the service down
questions.explain: Denial of wallet targets cost rather than availability — it exploits the fact that request-count limits don't account for how much compute (and therefore money) each individual AI call actually consumes.

questions.q: What should a token-based rate limit track, in addition to or instead of raw request count?
options: Only the caller's IP address, regardless of request content
Consumed or estimated input and output tokens against a rolling cost budget per caller
Only the time of day the requests arrive
The number of database tables the request touches
questions.explain: Measuring tokens or estimated compute cost over a rolling window lets a system throttle once a caller's cost budget is exhausted, not just once a request count is exhausted — closing the gap a denial-of-wallet attack exploits.

questions.q: Why does a model's response need an output-filtering stage before it reaches the caller?
options: Output filtering only matters for image-generating models, not text models
Model output is always identical to the exact prompt that was sent, so no new checks are needed

Generated text can contain things that weren't supposed to leave the system — leaked content from an access-control bug, reproduced PII, or raw markup that becomes a client-side risk if rendered untrusted
Output filtering is unnecessary once input validation has been applied
questions.explain: Because a response is generated text rather than a value the application constructed, it needs its own security check on the way out: content screening, schema validation, and safe handling of any markup the client will render.
